description: AKA Ignition is a focused, three-person development team composed of first-year Computer Science and Engineering students driven to solve complex aerospace challenges through intuitive AI applications. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, the team is exclusively tackling the "Flame in Freefall" problem statement by engineering a modern, full-stack web dashboard that translates decades of dense microgravity combustion data into accessible, actionable fire safety insights.
summary: Flame in Freefall (AstroFlame SI) is an interactive spacecraft fire-safety intelligence dashboard and hybrid RAG engine developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We engineered a data pipeline synthesizing over 150,000 rows of raw NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion telemetry—spanning experiments like FLEX, SAME-R, BASS-II, and SAFFIRE-1—into a structured relational database. Built with Streamlit and pure NumPy, the platform features a zero-hallucination hybrid retriever (85% semantic vector similarity + 15% lexical keyword boost) paired with Gemini, alongside an environmental simulator modeling oxygen levels, ventilation airflow, and fractional gravity regimes ($0g$ to $1g$).  AstroFlame SI addresses the critical challenge of predicting counter-intuitive microgravity combustion physics, where buoyancy vanishes, smoke fails to rise, and low-temperature "cool flames" burn quasi-steadily. By translating dense experimental telemetry into instant flammability risk indices, flame spread metrics, and suppression protocols, it empowers spacecraft engineers to qualify interior materials and design fail-safe detection systems—while accelerating terrestrial spinoffs in cleanroom monitoring and aircraft fire suppression.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Flame in Freefall (AstroFlame SI) is an interactive spacecraft fire-safety intelligence dashboard and custom Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) engine. It acts as an aerospace engineering co-pilot, predicting and analyzing combustion behavior in environments where traditional physics (like buoyancy and convection) break down.

The system operates on three core pillars:

  • Data Synthesis Pipeline: We ingested a 27 MB multi-sheet workbook containing over 150,000 rows of raw NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) telemetry (spanning experiments like FLEX, SAME-R, BASS-II, and SAFFIRE-1). We programmatically cleaned, aggregated, and normalized this high-frequency sensor data, droplet histories, and micro-pillar mechanical metrics into a flat, relational JSON schema linking investigations, tested materials, and terrestrial spinoffs.
  • Hybrid In-Memory RAG Engine: Instead of relying on generic keyword searches or heavy third-party vector databases, we built a custom search algorithm in pure NumPy. It combines an 85% semantic cosine similarity search (powered by Google Gemini embeddings) with a 15% lexical keyword boost. This ensures the AI understands the conceptual physics of a query while perfectly matching exact acronyms (e.g., "PMMA", "SAME-R").
  • Telemetry Simulator Interface: The Streamlit UI features a "Mission Control" sidebar where users can adjust Oxygen (%), Fractional Gravity ($0g$ to $1g$), Airflow, and Pressure. The dashboard dynamically updates to display the dominant flame regime (e.g., spherical diffusion vs. buoyant plume), calculates flammability risk, and generates Plotly data visualizations comparing material flame spread rates.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Spacecraft fire safety relies on understanding highly counter-intuitive microgravity phenomena—such as smoke that fails to rise and low-temperature "cool flames" that burn invisibly after hot-flame extinction.

AstroFlame SI bridges the gap between decades of dense, isolated NASA research and rapid engineering application. It empowers mission architects to instantly qualify interior materials, design zero-convection smoke detection protocols, and understand flame extinction limits. Beyond space exploration, the platform emphasizes Earth applications, surfacing NASA spinoffs like low-flow gaseous fire suppression for commercial aircraft cargo holds and particle detection systems for highly controlled terrestrial cleanrooms and data centers.

Tools, Technologies, and Hardware

  • Programming Language: Python 3
  • Frontend UI/UX: Streamlit (featuring custom injected "Space & Flame" glassmorphic CSS)
  • Data Engineering & Math: NumPy, Pandas, JSON, Pickle (persistent disk caching)
  • Data Visualization: Plotly (plotly.express, plotly.graph_objects)
  • AI & LLM Integration: Google Gemini SDK (v1beta), utilizing text-embedding-004 for vector generation and gemini-2.5-flash for grounded conversational extraction.
  • Hardware: Developed entirely locally on a consumer Lenovo ThinkPad (AMD Ryzen AI 7 450, 16GB DDR5 RAM), proving that heavy enterprise AI architecture can be deployed on edge devices with zero cloud-compute budget.

Creativity & Factors Considered

The Zero-Hallucination Constraint: In aerospace engineering, fabricated data is fatal. We strictly constrained our LLM generation by feeding the exact quantitative metrics extracted from the PSI data (e.g., $1.8\text{ mm/s}$ flame spread, $0.328\text{ mm}^2\text{/s}$ burning rate constants) directly into the hybrid context window. If the data is absent, the engine explicitly declines to answer rather than hallucinating.

Overcoming Hardware & API Bottlenecks: We initially hit 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED rate limits while sending thousands of tokens of scraped experimental data to the embedding API. We creatively solved this by engineering an asynchronous batch-embedding pipeline with token truncation ([:8000]), backed by a .pkl local disk cache. This allowed the app to launch instantly and run the RAG offline without repeatedly pinging the cloud.

Algorithmic Efficiency: By L2-normalizing our vectors upon ingestion, we reduced the complex cosine similarity math to a lightning-fast NumPy dot product. This eliminated the need for paid cloud vector databases (like Pinecone or Weaviate), achieving enterprise-grade hybrid retrieval entirely in local RAM.
